claims.text: Retention of toughness in near-equiatomic, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys is governed by the stability of the FCC matrix against thermally induced brittle intermetallic precipitation.
Controlled thermal aging can produce brittle intermetallic precipitates in the FCC matrix.
A critical precipitate volume fraction exists above which precipitates impede dislocation mobility.
Impeded dislocation mobility reduces the alloy's capacity for plastic deformation.
Reduced plastic deformation causes a marked loss of toughness.
Thermal aging promotes the nucleation and growth of brittle intermetallic phases.
At low precipitate fractions, precipitation may cause minor increases in strength.
Above the critical precipitate fraction, loss of ductility predominates over any strengthening benefit.
The relevant intermetallic precipitates are nanoscale and form particularly along grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
Samples aged to a precipitate fraction above the critical threshold will have significantly lower fracture toughness than the as-cast baseline.
The proposed initial state is a homogeneous, near-equiatomic, single-phase FCC alloy with negligible brittle precipitates.
The as-cast or minimally processed baseline is assumed to have a stable, ductile FCC microstructure with minimal precipitate formation.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to near-equiatomic, initially single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys aged under service-relevant conditions.
The hypothesis may not apply to alloys with different crystal structures or pre-existing multiphase microstructures.
The critical precipitate volume fraction is alloy-dependent and is not presently defined.
